section.title: Haman's Plot Against the Jews
section.sectionRationale: The danger arrives. Haman the Agagite is promoted to second in the empire, and when Mordecai the Jew will not bow, Haman's wounded pride swells into a plan to exterminate every Jew in the kingdom. He casts lots for the date, buys a genocidal decree from a careless king, and seals it with the royal signet. An ancient enmity, Amalek against Israel, flares into a death sentence for the whole covenant people, published across the empire in a single day.
section.thesis: One man's pride, backed by an old satanic hatred of God's people and an irreversible pagan law, sets a genocide in motion; the covenant people are condemned to death, and only the God who is never named can turn it back.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Haman exalted and Mordecai unbowed; the casting of the lot; Haman purchasing a decree of destruction; and the death decree sent through the empire.

verses.text: After these events, King Xerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, the {{agagi|Agagite}}, elevating him to a position above all the princes who were with him.
All the royal servants at the king’s gate bowed down and paid {{shachah|homage}} to Haman, because the king had commanded that this be done for him. But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage.
Then the royal servants at the king’s gate asked Mordecai, “Why do you disobey the command of the king?”
Day after day they warned him, but he would not comply. So they reported it to Haman to see whether Mordecai’s behavior would be tolerated, since he had told them he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, he was filled with rage.

And when he learned the identity of Mordecai’s people, he scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone. Instead, he sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes.

units.label: The lot is cast
units.note: a date chosen by chance, ruled from heaven

verses.text: In the twelfth year of King Xerxes, in the first month, the month of Nisan, the {{pur|Pur}} (that is, the lot) was cast before Haman to determine a day and month. And the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

units.label: Haman buys a genocide
units.note: a lie, a bribe, and a signet ring

verses.text: Then Haman informed King Xerxes, “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws. So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them.
If it pleases the king, let a decree be issued to destroy them, and I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury to pay those who carry it out.”
So the king removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
“Keep your money,” said the king to Haman. “These people are given to you to do with them as you please.”

units.label: The death decree goes out
units.note: a whole people condemned in a day

verses.text: On the thirteenth day of the first month, the royal scribes were summoned and the order was written exactly as Haman commanded the royal satraps, the governors of each province, and the officials of each people, in the script of each province and the language of every people. It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the royal signet ring.

And the letters were sent by couriers to each of the royal provinces with the order to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews, young and old, women and children, and to plunder their possessions on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month.
A copy of the text of the edict was to be issued in every province and published to all the people, so that they would be ready on that day.
The couriers left, spurred on by the king’s command, and the edict was issued in the citadel of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.

agagi.gloss: Agagite, marking Haman as a descendant, or at least a symbolic heir, of Agag, king of the Amalekites, 1 Samuel 15. Amalek was Israel's ancient enemy, sworn against by God, Exodus 17:16. Mordecai, a Benjamite son of Kish, stands in the line of Saul, so the old war between Israel and Amalek flares again in a Persian court.

shachah.gloss: To bow down, prostrate, or pay homage, the same verb used for worship. Mordecai's refusal to bow is likely more than rudeness: to prostrate before an Agagite, the sworn enemy of God's people, would betray his identity and his God. His stand triggers Haman's rage and the whole crisis.

pur.gloss: The Pur, a lot or die cast to choose a lucky day, an Akkadian loanword the narrator explains as the lot. Haman trusts chance to time his slaughter, but Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap, yet its every decision is from the LORD. The feast of Purim will take its name from this very word.

basic.context: The threat now takes shape. The king promotes Haman to the highest place under the throne and commands everyone to bow to him. Mordecai the Jew will not. Enraged, and despising the idea of punishing one man, Haman resolves to wipe out Mordecai's entire people. He casts lots to pick the date, then sells the king a lie, a troublesome people who do not obey the laws, and offers a fortune for permission to destroy them. The king hands over his signet ring and waves off the money. A decree goes out across the empire: on one day, kill every Jew, young and old, women and children. Then the king and Haman sit down to drink while the city reels.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not simply court intrigue; it is the latest round in an ancient war. Haman is an Agagite, heir of Amalek, Israel's sworn enemy; Mordecai descends from Saul's line. The narrator wants us to feel the deep, almost cosmic hatred behind the plot, and to notice how casually monstrous evil can become when pride meets power. The pressing question is God's hiddenness at its darkest: where is He when a decree of genocide is sealed and the king toasts it with wine? The book's answer, still unspoken, is that even the lot falls under His hand.
basic.originalLanguages: The word Agagite ties Haman to Agag the Amalekite, and the old command that Israel and Amalek would be at war from age to age. Mordecai refuses to bow, shachah, the verb for homage and worship, because bowing to this enemy would deny his people and his God. And Haman casts the Pur, the lot, trusting chance, though Scripture insists the lot's every outcome is from the LORD. From that word Pur the Jews will one day name their festival of rescue, Purim.
basic.typology: Haman is a vivid picture of the serpent's ongoing war on the seed of the woman, the recurring attempt to destroy the covenant people and, through them, cut off the promised Messiah. The condemned Jews, sentenced to death by an irreversible law they cannot escape, foreshadow all humanity under the sentence of sin. Their only hope is a deliverer who can overturn a doom that looks final.
basic.christ: Behind Haman stands the ancient enemy who has always sought to destroy God's people and stop the coming of Christ, from Pharaoh's slaughter of the Hebrew boys to Herod's slaughter at Bethlehem. Every such plot fails, because God guards the line of the Messiah. And the death sentence hanging over the Jews, an unchangeable law demanding their destruction, mirrors the law that condemns us all; only in Christ is an irreversible sentence answered by a greater deliverance.
basic.god: God is never named, and the horror is left to stand: a genocide decreed, the enemy and the king drinking together. Yet even here God is not absent. The lot that sets the date falls, unknown to Haman, on the far end of the year, giving time for rescue. The very irreversibility that dooms the Jews will trap Haman too. God rules the pride of men and the fall of the dice, and He will not let His people be destroyed.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 17 records the LORD's war with Amalek from generation to generation. Proverbs 16 says the lot is cast, but its decision is from the LORD. Genesis 3 promises enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed. And Revelation 12 shows the dragon waging war on God's people, always defeated.
basic.oneStory: An old satanic hatred, embodied in an Agagite's pride, wins a death sentence for the whole covenant people. It is the serpent's endless war on the seed of the woman, and it looks, for now, unstoppable. But the God who rules even the lot has already timed His rescue, and the line that leads to the Messiah will not be cut off.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 is the book's hinge, the point where a court comedy becomes a matter of life and death. The chapter is arranged in a tight sequence of cause and effect: promotion, refusal, rage, plan, accusation, permission, decree, and a final image. The first half, verses 1 to 6, is driven by two people who will not yield, Haman who demands homage and Mordecai who will not give it. The second half, verses 7 to 15, is bureaucratic and cold, a sequence of lots, dates, money, seals and couriers.

The author sets several contrasts side by side. Haman is honoured 'above all the princes,' verse 1, and yet a single man's refusal fills him with rage, verse 5. The plan he devises is disproportionate, 'all of Mordecai's people,' verse 6, and the language of the decree, 'destroy, kill, and annihilate,' verse 13, piles up three verbs of death. The phrase will return, turned around, in Esther 7:4 and 8:11.

The chapter's final sentence is one of the most chilling in the book: 'the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.' The banquet motif returns, and it is set against a city in dismay. The feast in chapter 1 ended in the removal of a queen; this one ends in a death warrant for a people.

The narrator also works with dates. The lot is cast in the first month, verse 7, the decree is written on the thirteenth day of the first month, verse 12, and the slaughter is set for the thirteenth of the twelfth month, verse 13. The gap of nearly a year leaves space for the events of the next chapters. The chapter closes without a word about the Jews' response, and that silence is loud.
context.historical:
The 'twelfth year' of Xerxes, verse 7, is about 474 BC, five years after Esther became queen. Haman's title, the Agagite, connects him with Agag, the Amalekite king of 1 Samuel 15. The Amalekites had attacked Israel in the wilderness, Exodus 17:8 to 16, and the LORD had sworn to war against them from generation to generation. Whether Haman was a literal descendant or was called an Agagite in a wider sense, the author wants readers to hear the old enmity.

Bowing before officials was a normal part of Persian court life, and to kneel and prostrate oneself before a superior was common. Jews elsewhere in the Bible bowed to kings and others without a problem, as Nathan did before David, 1 Kings 1:23. For that reason Mordecai's refusal is a puzzle. The text says only that he would not bow and that the reason was linked to his being a Jew, verse 4. Different readers have thought he refused because Haman was an Amalekite, because the honour bordered on worship, or because of a principle about giving to a man what belongs to God.

Casting lots was a widespread way of choosing days. The word 'Pur' is not Hebrew, and the author glosses it, 'that is, the lot,' verse 7, for readers who would not know it. It is an Akkadian word, and the gloss shows that the book was written for readers at a distance from Persian court life. The month chosen, Adar, is the twelfth, so the Jews had almost a year.

The royal signet ring, verse 10, was the king's authority in wax, and to give it away was to hand over the power to issue binding edicts, as Pharaoh did to Joseph, Genesis 41:42. The decree went by courier in every language and script, as the empire's postal system allowed, and the sum of ten thousand talents of silver was a vast figure. The king refused it, verse 11, which some read as an easy dismissal of the matter, and others as a polite way of accepting.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on the oldest enmity in the Old Testament. The Amalekites were the first to attack Israel after the exodus, Exodus 17:8, and Deuteronomy 25:17 to 19 commands Israel to remember and to blot out their memory. Saul's failure to finish the task, 1 Samuel 15, cost him the kingdom. When Haman is called the Agagite and Mordecai, the Kishite, the reader hears the old story reopened. The book of Esther takes the conflict to its conclusion and shows in Esther 9:10 and 15 that the Jews, unlike Saul, took no plunder.

Behind Haman's plan lies the pattern of Pharaoh in Exodus 1, who tried to destroy Israel by killing the children. Haman goes further and plans to kill every Jew. Scripture also gives a wider frame: the serpent's enmity with the woman's seed, Genesis 3:15, is repeated in every attempt to wipe out the people of the promise. Psalm 83:4 records the cry, 'Come, let us wipe them out as a nation,' and Psalm 124:1 to 3 says that if the LORD had not been on Israel's side, they would have been swallowed alive.

The New Testament takes up the themes. The rage of a proud man against one who will not bow is echoed by Herod's slaughter of children, Matthew 2:16, and by the powers behind Revelation 12:13 to 17, where the dragon pursues the woman and her offspring. Paul teaches that our struggle is not against flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12. The scriptures show that the enemy of God's people is older and larger than Haman, and that the LORD's promise to preserve them stands.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted readers to understand the danger their people had faced and how quickly and casually it arose. A whole community is condemned because one man's pride was hurt, and the decree is issued by men who eat and drink while a city is in shock. He wanted them to see that hatred can be dressed as policy: Haman does not say he is angry, he says the Jews are different and that the king's interest requires their removal, verses 8 and 9. It is the pattern of prejudice presented as reasonable.

He also wanted them to see that the danger was beyond their power to prevent. There is no army, no prophet and no appeal in the chapter, only a law that cannot be repealed. The reader is meant to feel that nothing but God can save the Jews, and to notice that His name is absent. The whole book turns on that silence.

The author also wanted readers to notice what Mordecai does not explain. He simply will not bow. In a book of hidden things, the one open act of conscience sets off the crisis. The author lets that stand as an example of a person who holds his line at cost, without telling us the whole reason.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a plot, a lot, a decree and an act of refusal. None of it is offered as instruction. Haman's reasoning is wicked, the king's careless consent is condemned by the narrator's tone, and the couriers are servants of an evil order. The chapter does not command believers to defy authority whenever they dislike it. Scripture elsewhere tells Christians to honour those in authority, Romans 13:1 to 7 and 1 Peter 2:13 to 17, and also to obey God rather than men, Acts 5:29. Mordecai's refusal fits the second principle if his refusal was conscience, but the text does not say so directly and we should be modest in applying it.

What is clear is the teaching that evil planned against God's people does not escape His notice. The chapter shows how quickly ordinary bureaucracy can be turned into a machine of death, and it invites the reader to watch for that in every age. It also shows the cost of a public stand. Mordecai did not know that his refusal would put a whole people at risk, and the book does not ask us to praise him for that. What it asks is that we trust God in circumstances where the outcome is unclear.

debates.question: Why would Mordecai not bow to Haman?

views.label: Because Haman was an Amalekite
views.case: Mordecai was descended from Kish, and Haman from Agag. The ancient hostility, Exodus 17:14 to 16, and Saul's failure, 1 Samuel 15, give the confrontation a covenant setting, and bowing to an Amalekite would have been to submit to the enemy the LORD had sworn to fight.

views.label: Because the homage bordered on worship
views.case: The verbs 'bow down and pay homage' are the same ones used elsewhere of worship, and the king had commanded it for Haman, verse 2. A Jew who would give obeisance only to God, Exodus 20:3 to 5, might refuse such honour. Later Jewish tradition has often read it this way.

views.label: Personal principle and pride
views.case: The text gives no reason beyond the fact that Mordecai was a Jew, verse 4. Some think Mordecai was stubborn or proud, since Jews elsewhere bowed to rulers, and the narrator does not commend him. The book does not settle the point.

debates.bearing: The narrator ties the refusal to Mordecai's identity as a Jew and to the older story of Kish and Agag, and that is the safest ground. Whatever the mix of his motives, the book presents his stand as the occasion of an attack that God will turn back, and it does not make us judge his heart.

debates.question: Is the plot against the Jews about ethnic hatred or religious difference?

views.label: Ancient antisemitism
views.case: Haman's speech in verse 8, that the Jews are scattered, that their laws differ and that they do not obey the king's laws, is a classic pattern of prejudice against a minority. Many readers see it as the earliest literary picture of a genocidal decree against Jews.

views.label: A spiritual conflict with old roots
views.case: Others emphasize that Haman's roots in Amalek make this the latest round of an ancient battle between the seed of the promise and its enemies, Genesis 3:15 and Exodus 17:16. The immediate cause is a slight, but the deeper source is the enmity Scripture describes across the ages.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. Haman's speech is the ordinary language of prejudice, and behind it lies the older enmity. The author lets both be true and shows that God's covenant with His people stands over both.

study.originalLanguages:
Haman's rage in verse 5 is described with the ordinary word for fury, chemah, and he is 'filled' with it. The book's first chapter had used the same word of Xerxes, whose 'anger burned within him,' Esther 1:12. The king's fury cost him a queen, and Haman's rage will cost him his life, and by using the same term the author draws the two men together.

When the servants bow, the verb pair in verses 2 and 5 is kara' and hishtachavah, 'kneel' and 'bow down.' The second is the standard word for both homage to a superior and worship of God, and the book uses them together. The text says Mordecai would not kneel or prostrate himself, and the same pair is used when Haman is honoured. The ambiguity of the verb is part of why readers have asked whether the act was a civil courtesy or a religious one.

Verse 6 says Haman thought it beneath him to 'lay hands' on Mordecai alone, a phrase from the language of violence, shalach yad, literally to send out a hand. The narrator comments that he scorned the idea in his eyes, and the reader hears the smallness of his pride. The plan grows to fill the whole empire because his hurt is larger than one man.

The word Pur in verse 7 is not Hebrew, and the narrator translates it, 'that is, the lot.' Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap but every decision is from the LORD. The book will later name the festival Purim from it, Esther 9:26. The word reminds the reader that what looks like chance is in God's hand, and it is a striking ironic touch that Haman uses the lot to pick the day of the Jews' destruction and it falls on the twelfth month, giving time for the rescue.

Haman's accusation in verse 8 uses two participles, mefuzar and meforad, 'scattered and dispersed.' They are near synonyms, and the pairing is a piece of rhetoric, making the Jews seem both everywhere and separate. It echoes the language of Deuteronomy 28:64, where the LORD warned that He would scatter His people among the nations. The scattering that was a judgment now becomes the excuse for the attack.

He adds that their laws, data, differ from those of every people and that they do not keep the king's laws, using the same word for law that the book uses for royal decrees. The claim is a distortion, since Mordecai had helped the king by exposing a plot, Esther 2:22, but it sounds plausible and strikes at what a Persian king would fear.

Finally, verse 10 calls Haman 'the enemy of the Jews,' tsorer. It is the root of the LORD's promise in Exodus 23:22 to be 'an enemy to your enemies,' from the same word. The narrator chooses a covenant word for Haman and so quietly sets the LORD on the other side of the conflict.

typology.type: Haman, the enemy who seeks to destroy the people of the promise
typology.fulfillment: Haman plans to destroy every Jew, as Pharaoh once tried to destroy Israel's sons, Exodus 1:15-22, and as Herod tried to destroy the newborn Christ, Matthew 2:16. Behind them stands the serpent who has been at war with the woman's offspring from the start, Genesis 3:15, and the dragon of Revelation 12:4 who waits to devour the child. Christ fulfils the pattern by being the promised seed who could not be destroyed, and by dying and rising He broke the power of the enemy, Hebrews 2:14. The type falls short because Haman is a man with limited power, and the true adversary is not flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12.

The edict sealed with the king's ring cannot be recalled, and it condemns a whole people to die on a set day. Scripture treats the sentence of death on humanity as a fixed decree, Romans 5:12 and 6:23, which none can undo by their own effort. In Christ the sentence is met and answered, since He bore it Himself, Colossians 2:14 says the record of debt against us was nailed to the cross. The comparison is loose and must not be pressed: Xerxes' decree was unjust, but the judgment on sin is just, and the way it is resolved is that the judge himself takes the penalty.

typology.type: The lot cast to fix a day and month
typology.fulfillment: Haman casts the Pur to choose the day, and the lot falls in a way he cannot control. Proverbs 16:33 says the decision belongs to the LORD. The pattern points to Christ as the one whose hour is fixed by the Father: 'My time is not yet here,' John 7:8, and 'the hour has come,' John 12:23. The lot cast for His clothing at the cross, John 19:24, recalls Psalm 22:18. The type is limited in that it concerns a plot and not a plan of salvation, and Haman's lot is turned against him by God, not chosen by God as the death of Christ was.

study.christ:
Esther 3 does not mention Christ, and we should not force a reading of it. It leads toward Him in three careful ways: by showing the enemy of the promise, by showing the kind of sentence hanging over God's people, and by revealing what kind of rescue would be needed.

The first is the enemy. The Bible's story is one of a war between the seed of the woman and the serpent, Genesis 3:15, and every generation sees an attempt to destroy the line through which the promise comes. Pharaoh tried, Athaliah tried, 2 Kings 11:1, Herod tried, Matthew 2:16, and Haman tried here. The book of Esther is the account of one such attempt that failed, and it matters for the gospel because the Messiah was to come from this people, Romans 9:5. If Haman had succeeded, the promise to Abraham would have had no heirs. The story is therefore a step in the long preservation of the line that leads to Bethlehem.

The second is the decree. A sentence of death hangs over a whole people, sealed and unalterable, and there is nothing they can do to change it. This is not the same as the gospel, but it is a picture of the human condition as Paul describes it: we were dead in our trespasses and could not save ourselves, Ephesians 2:1 to 5. The good news is that the Judge Himself provided the way. Colossians 2:14 says that God cancelled the written code that stood against us, taking it away and nailing it to the cross.

The third is the need for a mediator. The book will go on to show Esther approaching the king unsummoned on behalf of her people. Her intercession, at the risk of her life, is a shadow of a greater one. Christ 'always lives to intercede' for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25, and He has entered heaven itself to appear in God's presence for us, Hebrews 9:24. Where Esther risked death by going to an earthly king, Christ passed through death to bring us to the Father, and the sentence that stood against us was borne by Him.

We should be careful with the details. Haman is not a code for Satan in every respect, Mordecai is not Christ, and Esther is not a saviour in the way Jesus is. The links are those of theme and pattern: the enemy who cannot succeed against the promise, the decree that no human power can revoke, and the mediator who stands before a king. The chapter's silence about God is the reason the New Testament matters, since it says openly what Esther can only imply, that God has acted to rescue, Titus 3:4 to 5.
study.god:
God does not appear in the chapter, and yet the chapter is full of the questions He alone can answer. A whole people is condemned by an unrepealable law, and a proud man has been given the king's ring. If the book only told this story, it would be a story of despair. It teaches instead that the God of the covenant is the one who governs the lots, the kings and the couriers, and the way it shows this is by irony.

First, the lot. Haman casts the Pur to find a lucky day and month. The book says, without comment, that the lot fell on the twelfth month, the last, and this gave almost a year for the plot to be undone. Proverbs 16:33 explains what the narrator leaves unsaid: 'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.' God's sovereignty extends even to the throw of the dice, and He is not the prisoner of the schemes of those who oppose Him.

Second, the covenant. The narrator calls Haman 'the enemy of the Jews,' using the root of the LORD's own promise to be 'an enemy to your enemies,' Exodus 23:22. The choice of word is quiet, but it puts God on the side of His people even when they do not know it. The promise to Abraham, 'I will curse those who treat you with contempt,' Genesis 12:3, is being tested here, and it will not fail. The chapter shows the LORD as a faithful covenant God, whose loyalty does not depend on His people's awareness of it.

Third, the tension between evil and providence. God does not cause Haman's hatred, and the book does not treat it as good. Yet He is not surprised by it and He does not let it have the last word. Scripture keeps both in view: human beings are accountable for their malice, and God rules over it, Acts 2:23. Psalm 33:10 says the LORD frustrates the plans of the nations, and Psalm 2 says He laughs at the kings who scheme against Him. The chapter's dark humour carries the same conviction, that a plot laid with a king's seal is no match for God's purpose.

For worship, the chapter teaches trust when the situation looks hopeless. It gives permission to feel the confusion of Susa in verse 15 and yet to hope. It also teaches humility. The proud man who was honoured above all the princes is the one who will be undone, and God resists the proud, James 4:6. The God who is silent is not absent, and the believer is called to trust Him in the silence.

crossReferences.note: Amalek attacks Israel in the wilderness, and the LORD says He will war against Amalek from generation to generation. It gives Haman the Agagite his ancestry of enmity, and shows that the conflict in Esther 3 is an old one carried into a Persian court.

Saul spares Agag and the best of the spoil, and loses his kingdom for it. The failure explains why the descendant of Agag is still alive in Esther 3:1, and why Mordecai, a descendant of Saul's family, stands in the story to finish what Saul left undone.

Israel is told to remember what Amalek did and to blot out the memory of Amalek. It shows why Mordecai's refusal to honour an Agagite would carry a covenant weight, and why the book sets the two in such open conflict.

A proverb about dice thrown in the lap, with the verdict belonging to the LORD. It supplies the theology behind Haman's Pur in Esther 3:7, and explains why the lot's outcome, the twelfth month, gives time for the rescue.

Pharaoh gives Joseph his signet ring and so hands him authority to act. Xerxes' gift of the ring to Haman in Esther 3:10 is the dark counterpart, a ring given for salvation in one story and for slaughter in the other.

Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys killed to break Israel's growth. Haman's decree is larger, aimed at every Jew, and the parallel places his plot in the long line of attempts to destroy the people of the promise.

The LORD promises to be an enemy to Israel's enemies. The Hebrew word for enemy used here is the root behind the description of Haman as the enemy of the Jews in Esther 3:10, and it hints that God has taken the other side.
The LORD warns that He will scatter His people among all the nations. Haman's words in Esther 3:8 describe the same scattering as a reason to destroy them, turning a judgment into an excuse.
If the LORD had not been on our side, when men attacked us, they would have swallowed us alive. It voices what Esther 3 leaves unsaid, that only the LORD stands between His people and total loss.

The first promise of a woman's offspring who will strike the serpent. Haman's plot is one of many attempts to destroy the line of promise, and Genesis 3:15 explains why such attempts recur throughout the Bible.
The dragon pursues the woman and makes war on her other children. It shows Haman's kind of hatred as an episode in a larger conflict, and it promises that the dragon's pursuit ends in defeat.

Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of evil. It teaches readers to see that behind human enemies like Haman there stands a greater adversary, whom only Christ finally overcomes.

study.oneStory:
Esther 3 stands at the moment in the story of the Bible where the enemy's attack is at its widest. God's promise to Abraham was of a people and a blessing for all nations, Genesis 12:1 to 3, and the enmity foretold in Genesis 3:15 has followed that promise through every age. Here the whole surviving people, in every province, is marked for a single day of death. The chapter answers the question, 'what happens to the promise when its people are scattered and powerless?' with a plain picture of how exposed they are.

The chapter also looks back. Amalek attacked Israel just after the exodus, when they were weary, Deuteronomy 25:18, and the LORD had vowed to blot out that memory. Saul was sent to do it and failed, and the failure has a descendant, Haman, who stands in the palace. The story of Esther shows that the promise of the LORD stands even when human failure lets an old enemy live. What Saul left undone becomes the setting of a rescue that God brings about through a very different route.

What it sets up is the reversal. The three verbs of Haman's decree, destroy, kill and annihilate, will come back in Esther 7:4 in Esther's mouth and in 8:11 in the Jews' permission to defend themselves. The lot, the ring, the couriers and the banquet all return in altered form. It also sets up the mediator, since chapter 4 will show Esther, once silent, taking her place before the king. The way the plot is built suggests a larger truth: that God's rescue often comes by turning the enemy's own instruments against him.

The story leads at last to the cross and to new creation. Haman's decree condemned a people to die on one day, and Christ took a decree of death on Himself, Colossians 2:14, so that His people should not perish. The dragon who makes war on the woman's offspring is finally cast out, Revelation 12:9 to 11 and 20:10. In the new creation there is no more death or mourning, Revelation 21:4, and no decree that can reach the people of God. The city that was in confusion in Susa is replaced by a city of peace, and those who were marked for slaughter are found in the Lamb's book of life, Revelation 21:27.

sermon.title: God Is in Charge
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this message expounds Esther 3:1-15, Haman's promotion, Mordecai's refusal, and the murderous decree, holding out the sovereignty of the unseen God over even a sealed sentence of death. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What set Haman's murderous plan in motion?

options.text: Mordecai's refusal to bow, which enraged Haman and led him to target all the Jews.
options.note: Esther 3:2-6 shows Haman's rage at Mordecai widening into a plot against the whole people.

options.text: A direct command from the king to destroy the Jews.
options.note: The king only later approved Haman's scheme; the plot began with Haman's wounded pride.

options.text: A famine that Haman blamed on the Jews.
options.note: There is no famine in the account; the trigger was Mordecai's refusal to bow.

options.text: The Jews attacking Haman first.
options.note: The Jews did nothing of the kind; Haman's aggression sprang from his own pride.

quiz.q: Why is it significant that Haman is called an Agagite?

options.text: It marks him as heir of Amalek, Israel's ancient sworn enemy, renewing an old, God-ordained conflict.
options.note: Agag was king of Amalek, 1 Samuel 15; the label signals a deep, ongoing enmity.

options.text: It means he was a foreigner with no history with Israel.
options.note: The opposite: it ties him to a long history of enmity with God's people.

options.text: It simply names his home province.
options.note: It is a lineage, not a mere geographic label; it carries the Amalekite feud.

options.text: It shows he was secretly a friend of the Jews.
options.note: He is called the enemy of the Jews; the term underlines his hostility.

quiz.q: How did Haman gain the king's approval for the decree?

options.text: He slandered the Jews as lawless and offered a vast bribe; the careless king gave him the signet ring.
options.note: Esther 3:8-11 records the lie, the offered silver, and the king's ring.

options.text: He proved in court that the Jews had committed crimes.
options.note: There was no proof, only slander; the charge was a manipulative lie.

options.text: He forced the king at swordpoint.
options.note: No force was used; the king was persuaded and indifferent.

options.text: He was refused and had to act on his own.
options.note: The king granted the request and handed over his ring.

quiz.q: What does the casting of the Pur reveal, in light of the whole book?

options.text: Haman trusted chance, but God rules the lot; the date fell far off, leaving room for rescue.
options.note: Proverbs 16:33 and the plot both show God's hidden hand over the lot.

options.text: That the date was chosen by careful strategy, not chance.
options.note: It was chosen by lot; the point is God's rule over that chance.

options.text: That God had no involvement in the timing.
options.note: The narrative implies the opposite: the timing serves God's rescue.

options.text: That the Jews had already been destroyed.
options.note: The lot set a future date; the danger, and the rescue, still lay ahead.

quiz.q: How does the plot against the Jews connect to the larger biblical story?

options.text: It is another attempt in the serpent's war to destroy God's people and cut off the line to the Messiah, and it fails.
options.note: Like Pharaoh and Herod, Haman's plot is the enemy's assault on the covenant line, always defeated.

options.text: It shows that God's promises to His people had finally failed.
options.note: The opposite: the rescue proves the promises hold.

options.text: It is an isolated event with no link to the rest of Scripture.
options.note: The Amalek and serpent themes tie it deeply into the whole story.

options.text: It proves the Jews were no longer God's people.
options.note: They remain the covenant people God preserves through the crisis.

questions: Haman's genocide grew out of one bruised ego. Where do you see wounded pride in your own heart, and where could it lead if left unchecked?
Mordecai would not bow, even when it was costly and dangerous. Where is God calling you to a faithful no that the world will not understand?
The king toasted a decree of death without a second thought. How does this scene expose the casual cruelty that power and comfort can breed, and where do you need to resist it?
The lot fell exactly where God meant it to, though Haman thought it was chance. How does it comfort you that God rules even the things that feel random in your life?
Behind Haman lies an ancient hatred of God's people that has always failed. How does knowing that evil is real, but already doomed, help you face opposition to your faith?

translationNotes.note: Agagite links Haman to Agag, king of the Amalekites, 1 Samuel 15, signaling the ancient enmity between Amalek and Israel that frames the conflict.
Pur is an Akkadian loanword for the lot, which the narrator explains; the feast of Purim in chapter nine takes its name from this word.
Ten thousand talents of silver is an enormous sum, roughly 342 metric tons, underscoring the scale of Haman's obsession and bribe.
The order to destroy young and old, women and children in a single day makes the decree an act of genocide, not judicial punishment.
